newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, pushing reforms, seeks entry into G7.
newsitem.headline: Russia, pushing reforms, seeks entry into G7.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin will seek entry to the Group of Seven leading industrial nations in Denver on Friday, leaving his government to battle on with the communist-dominated parliament over reform.
It will be the fifth time Yeltsin has joined a G7 summit, and this one will be officially titled the "Summit Of The Eight" in a nod to Russia's increasing role.

But the group -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- has not yet opened its doors fully to Moscow, and Yeltsin will be excluded from an hour of talks on financial and macro-economic issues.

"Of course, I am not only going to Denver to sort out the G8. But I do not want to hide from you that if the G8 question is finally resolved there, it would be a historic meeting for Russia," Yeltsin said before leaving for the Denver summit.
The Russian president's bid for a bigger summit role suffered a setback on Thursday when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he would oppose Russian participation in the financial talks.

"We are interested in seeing a consensus among G7 leaders that Russia will continue to be excluded from G7 talks on financial and macro-economic issues," Hashimoto told reporters on his plane to Denver.

Yeltsin, out of action for most of last year with heart problems and then pneumonia, will meet Hashimoto on Friday morning. He has made a big effort to reinvigorate reforms since he recovered in February and hopes to be rewarded by the West.

But the liberal ministers he appointed in March to lead the drive to remove the vestiges of central planning face fierce opposition from the communist-dominated lower house of parliament, which is appalled at their tough monetary plans.
On Friday the house, or State Duma, is set to return to the long-running issue of amendments to the 1997 budget which the government says are crucial to sort out chaotic finances.

Ministers wanted to slash spending by a fifth because of a shortfall in tax revenues, but parliament, afraid its long-suffering electorate will suffer from the spending squeeze, is insisting on much smaller cuts.
A special commission set up to try to overcome differences which have stalled passage of the bill failed to reach a compromise on Thursday, so parliament will discuss its own proposals on Friday.

The first would cut spending by 42 trillion roubles instead of the 88 trillion which the government wanted, while the second would let parliament off the hook by giving the government sole responsibility for meeting the 1997 budget.

The government says it will go ahead with its cuts regardless of parliament's decision, but wants deputies to approve the plan to show international lending organisations that legal processes count in this fledgling democracy.
The budget cutting plan is one of a series of bills which the cabinet is trying to force through parliament in the hope of dragging Russia from its deep post-communist recession.

Ministers scored a victory on Thursday when the chamber, subjected to a mixture of cajolery and threats from the government, gave its initial approval to a tax code which the International Monetary Fund sees as a key to further reform.
"This is a huge victory for us...This is also a big move for foreign businessmen," Yeltsin told reporters from G7 countries in an interview shown on Russia's commercial NTV.
He said lower taxes should help lure more foreign investors to Russia, which still suffers from an image of heavy-handed bureaucracy, rampant corruption and uncertain rules.
